_about: The hand-kept ledger of developments from 2024 on: date, who, what happened, what it does not mean, source id, confidence. Researched by a web agent on 2026-09-23 and edited by hand; rows marked unconfirmed rest on one secondary source. The weekly feed (recent.json) is separate and unread by a person. CC BY 4.0, Nan · hongdam.net.

rows.what: RSA-2048 with about 1,730 logical qubits by approximate residue arithmetic — a third of the usual count, at the price of about a thousand times more gates.
rows.not: Fewer qubits, far more time; a trade, not a shortcut.

rows.who: Wang Chao and others, Shanghai University
rows.what: A 22-bit RSA integer factored on a D-Wave annealer; in October the story runs worldwide as 'China breaks military-grade encryption'.
rows.not: 22 bits against 2048; annealing has no known scaling advantage; no key in use was affected.

rows.what: The first improvement since Ingham (1940) on how many zeta zeros can lie off the critical line in a range; published in the Annals in 2026.
rows.not: Progress on the Riemann Hypothesis, not a proof; no bearing on factoring.

rows.what: FIPS 203 (ML-KEM), 204 (ML-DSA) and 205 (SLH-DSA): the first final post-quantum standards.
rows.not: New locks on the shelf; nothing yet says when to take the old ones off.

rows.what: Twelve logical qubits on the 56-qubit H2 trapped-ion machine, with a 22-fold drop in circuit error against raw qubits.
rows.not: Twelve; a key break needs over a thousand, running billions of gates.

rows.what: Draft IR 8547: RSA-2048 and 256-bit curves deprecated after 2030, all quantum-vulnerable public-key algorithms disallowed after 2035.
rows.not: A policy calendar, not a forecast of when a machine arrives; still a draft in September 2026.

rows.what: Willow, 105 qubits: the first chip clearly below the error-correction threshold — logical error falls by about 2.1× each time the code grows a step, up to distance 7.
rows.not: One logical memory qubit, no logical gates; the 'ten septillion years' line is a sampling benchmark with nothing to do with factoring.

rows.what: 'A first successful factorization of RSA-2048 integer by D-Wave quantum computer', on 'a class of special integers'.
rows.not: The two primes differ in two low bits; Fermat's method from 1643 splits every such number in milliseconds. Not an RSA key.

rows.what: Majorana 1 announced as an eight-qubit topological processor.
rows.not: Nature's own editorial note said the paper does not show the topological states claimed; no error-corrected computation was shown.

rows.what: HQC chosen as a fifth post-quantum algorithm, a backup to ML-KEM built on different mathematics.
rows.not: Insurance against a lattice break, not a reaction to any factoring result.

rows.who: Wang Chao's group, via the South China Morning Post
rows.what: A 90-bit RSA integer reported factored on a D-Wave machine.
rows.not: No paper found; 90 bits is far below the 896-bit classical record.

rows.what: The Q-Day Prize: one bitcoin for the largest elliptic-curve key broken with Shor's algorithm on real hardware by 5 April 2026.
rows.not: Toy keys of 1 to 25 bits; a yardstick for hardware, not a measure of wallet risk.

rows.what: The Bitcoin report: about 6.26 million BTC (roughly 30%) sits in outputs whose public key is already visible; migrating every coin would take about 76 days of full blocks at best.
rows.not: A count of exposed keys, not of coins at risk today: no machine can use them yet.

rows.what: The iShares Bitcoin Trust prospectus adds that advances in quantum computing could undermine Bitcoin's cryptography and that any fix needs broad network consensus.
rows.not: Standard risk disclosure, as Bloomberg's ETF analyst said at the time.

rows.what: RSA-2048 with fewer than a million noisy qubits in under a week — a twentyfold drop from the 2019 figure, from better arithmetic, 'yoked' surface codes and cheaper magic states.
rows.not: Assumes 0.1% error and a microsecond cycle; the biggest machines have a hundred to a thousand qubits.

rows.what: Roadmap to Starling in 2029: 200 logical qubits and 100 million gates on qLDPC codes, via Loon (2025), Kookaburra (2026), Cockatoo (2027).
rows.not: Starling as described would still be below every published RSA-2048 budget.

rows.what: A 5-bit elliptic-curve key recovered with a Shor-style circuit on IBM's 133-qubit machine.
rows.not: A 32-element group; a pencil does it faster.

rows.who: Jameson Lopp, on the bitcoindev list
rows.what: A migration proposal: three years after a post-quantum output type exists, stop sending to legacy scripts; two years after that, stop accepting old signatures — freezing coins that did not move.
rows.not: A draft for discussion; no activation path.

rows.what: Helios: 98 trapped-ion qubits, 48 error-corrected logical qubits, two-qubit fidelity 99.92%.
rows.not: 48 logical qubits is a few percent of a key-breaking budget, and the runs are shallow.

rows.what: Nighthawk (120 qubits) and the experimental Loon chip with the long-range couplers qLDPC codes need.
rows.not: Physical-qubit devices; no logical factoring demonstration.

rows.what: An independent advisory board on quantum risk: Aaronson, Boneh, Drake, Kannan, Lindell, Malkhi.
rows.not: A board; its April paper says the threat is 'on the horizon' and blockchains are safe today.

rows.what: About 1.6 million BTC in exposed P2PK outputs, over 32,000 outputs of about 50 BTC each; the threat put at least a decade out.
rows.not: Counts only P2PK; reused addresses add millions more.

rows.what: BIP 360 becomes Pay-to-Merkle-Root (P2MR, addresses bc1z): Taproot's script tree with the key path removed. BIP 361 is Lopp's sunset schedule, numbered and merged as a draft in April.
rows.not: Both are drafts; neither has an activation path.

rows.what: 'Pinnacle': RSA-2048 with fewer than 100,000 physical qubits on qLDPC codes, about 22,000 at 0.01% error.
rows.not: Needs long-range connectivity and real-time decoding nobody has built; Aaronson: timeline effect unknown.

rows.who: Global Risk Institute — Mosca and Piani
rows.what: The 2025 expert survey: 26 experts put the chance of a 24-hour RSA-2048 break within ten years at 28–49%, the highest in the series; 92% give it even odds within twenty.
rows.not: Opinions of experts, weighted by how they were asked; not a date.

rows.what: Google will finish its own post-quantum migration by 2029, a year ahead of NIST's deprecation, citing hardware, error correction and the new resource estimates; Android 17 ships ML-DSA.
rows.not: A migration deadline, not a claim that RSA falls in 2029.

rows.who: Babbush, Zalcman, Gidney, Broughton, Khattar, Neven, Bergamaschi, Drake, Boneh
rows.what: A 256-bit curve key with under 1,450 logical qubits, 70–90 million Toffoli gates, fewer than 500,000 physical superconducting qubits, in 18–23 minutes — a twentyfold cut. Fast-clock machines could work inside Bitcoin's ten-minute block; ion and atom machines could not.
rows.not: A cost model; no such machine exists. Google withheld the circuits and published a zero-knowledge proof of their correctness instead.

rows.what: A neutral-atom machine of 10,000–26,000 physical qubits could break a 256-bit curve key, at about ten days per key.
rows.not: Atoms are a thousand times slower per step than superconducting qubits; days, not minutes.

rows.what: RSA-2048 in 9.2 days with 381,000 physical qubits by parking idle logical qubits in slower memory.
rows.not: Compiler accounting on assumed hardware; the '138×' headline is against a different baseline than Gidney 2025.

rows.what: A 'quantum canary': coins in an address only a quantum machine could open; a spend from it proves the capability and triggers restrictions on old wallets automatically.
rows.not: Critics: the first attacker may steal quietly rather than ring the bell.

rows.what: The Q-Day Prize awarded for a 15-bit curve key on IBM Heron processors.
rows.not: Bitcoin developers reproduced the result from random bits within a day; Project Eleven's CEO agreed it 'is not Q-Day'.

rows.what: Shor's algorithm compiled across a modular half-million-atom machine with 16% overhead against one module.
rows.not: An architecture study; no such machine.

rows.what: 6.04 million BTC (30.2%) with the spending key visible: 1.92 million structural (P2PK, Taproot), 4.12 million from address reuse, of which 1.66 million belongs to exchanges.
rows.not: Visible is not stolen; the count is of doors, not of thieves.

rows.what: About 7 million BTC exposed: 1.7 million in some 20,000 legacy P2PK addresses, about 5 million by address reuse, some in exchange cold wallets.
rows.not: Same doors, counted a third way.

rows.what: Federal high-value systems to move key establishment to post-quantum by end of 2030 and signatures by end of 2031.
rows.not: Applies to federal systems; says nothing new about machines.

rows.who: Jonas Nick and Mikhail Kudinov, Blockstream
rows.what: SHRINCS: a SHA-256-based post-quantum signature of about 324 bytes, sized so Bitcoin's throughput survives; demonstrated on Liquid in March.
rows.not: Security proof pending, no audit, needs a soft fork.

rows.what: States that 2^1277 − 1 (1,277 bits) was factored by the special number field sieve in September 2026.
rows.not: No announcement found on the usual lists; unverified.

rows.what: RSA-260 (862 bits) factored: CADO-NFS ported to GPUs with coding agents, 4,923 GPU-days on B200-class parts, about sixteen days elapsed.
rows.not: Lu: 'essentially no algorithmic advancements'. The sieve is the same; 2048 bits is not structurally closer.

rows.what: A blueprint: a 256-bit curve key in 25.7 days on 19,397 trapped-ion qubits (about 1,457 logical), 40 million Toffoli gates, 63% success.
rows.not: A design on paper; IonQ's largest machine is 256 qubits.

rows.what: RSA-896 (896 bits, 270 digits) factored with a GPU port of CADO-NFS, run as a low-priority job on up to 2,048 idle GPUs for ten days — about 30 GPU-years.
rows.not: Weis: no improvement to the number field sieve's running time and no effect on deployed RSA-2048; it does put RSA-1024 within reach of anyone with a data-centre GPU fleet.
